title: Supreme Court Bars Illegal Detentions, Orders Normal Metro and Internet in Delhi Protest Case
excerpt: A special Sunday bench barred illegal detention of peaceful protesters and ordered normal metro, rail and internet services after petitions alleged a crackdown on the October 10 anti-CEC protest.
body:
• In a rare special Sunday sitting, the Supreme Court ordered that no person be detained except in accordance with the procedure established by law, with particular protection for peaceful, unarmed protesters outside prohibitory-order zones.
  • The bench of Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana directed that Delhi Metro and rail services function normally, internet facilities remain undisturbed, and city barricades be reviewed and removed unless warranted.
  • The directions came on petitions alleging mass detentions and a shutdown of public transport during the October 10 protest at Jantar Mantar against Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar.
  • Solicitor General Tushar Mehta told the court the metro is fully functional, all stations are open and internet has been restored; the court issued notice to the Centre on the contempt plea.

The Supreme Court held a rare special sitting on Sunday and barred the illegal detention of peaceful protesters in Delhi, ordering the Centre and city authorities to restore normal metro, rail and internet services after allegations of a crackdown on the October 10 protest against Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar.

A bench of Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana directed that "there shall be no detention of any person except in accordance with the procedure established by law," particularly with respect to assemblies of peaceful and unarmed persons beyond areas where Section 163 BNSS prohibitory orders are in force. The interim directions are subject to law-and-order conditions, as contemplated under Article 19(2) of the Constitution.

"Senior counsels submitted there was a flagrant violation of the directions — metro railway was not functioning, New Delhi and Nizamuddin railway stations remained closed, no traffic advisories were issued and a large number of persons were subjected to undue harassment and illegal detention even beyond the area which was covered by the prohibitory order."

— The Supreme Court bench, in its order

What the court ordered

The court's directions, issued on urgent petitions over the policing of the Cockroach Janta Party's October 10 protest at Jantar Mantar against CEC Gyanesh Kumar over alleged election irregularities, covered four fronts:

https://x.com/WIONews/status/2109258344640983368

First, detentions: no illegal detention of peaceful protesters. Second, transport: metro and rail facilities must function normally unless restrictions are genuinely required for public order — not a blanket shutdown. Third, movement: free movement of people across the city subject to traffic regulations, with barricades reviewed "forthwith." Fourth, internet: connectivity must remain undisturbed, with Justice Bagchi orally clarifying that the court was not taking away the authorities' powers under the IT Act.

The bench also ordered the removal of a board announcing the imposition of Section 163 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita (BNSS) near the Supreme Court itself, if not already done, to remove any apprehension about access to justice — and asked Solicitor General Tushar Mehta to ensure lawyers, journalists and others are not impeded in their professional duties.

The petitions behind the sitting

The court assembled for the urgent hearing after advocate Shailendra Mani Tripathi filed a contempt petition alleging authorities had defied its October 9 order — issued in MA Baby v. Union of India — which had said transport restrictions for protests should be regulated and proportionate, not a complete prohibition. Separately, Trinamool Congress MP and senior advocate Menaka Guruswamy filed a habeas corpus petition challenging the preventive detention of opposition leaders, including four former chief ministers, rounded up before they could reach the protest venue.

According to the bench, senior counsel alleged metro services were not functioning, New Delhi and Nizamuddin railway stations remained closed, no traffic advisories were issued, and "a large number of persons were subjected to undue harassment and illegal detention even beyond the area" covered by the prohibitory order. Estimates of detentions during the October 10 crackdown have ranged from 1,000 to several thousand.

Government's response

SG Tushar Mehta assured the court that the metro railway has been functioning fully since 10 PM on October 10, all stations are open, trains are running normally and internet connectivity has been restored. He submitted that entry and exit were restricted at 45 out of 303 metro stations on October 10. The court issued notice to the Centre on the contempt plea.

What this means going forward

The directives set a judicial guardrail for Monday's planned opposition mobilisation — the INDIA bloc has called a march to Parliament Street and a delegation is to submit a memorandum to the Chief Justice of India. Any repeat of mass preventive detentions or transport shutdowns will now be measured against a court order issued on a Sunday sitting, not merely against earlier police assurances.

What's next

The court will hear the contempt plea further on notice to the Centre. With the opposition's October 12 mobilisation hours away, the next flashpoint is immediate: whether Monday's march proceeds under the court's new framework or triggers fresh confrontation on Delhi's streets.

Metro and rail services must function normally.
Barricades to be reviewed and removed.
